title: Closures and iterators
summary: Small inline functions, and chains that transform a collection.

blocks.html: A closure is a small function you write inline. The syntax swaps fn name(params) for two pipes around the parameters, and the body is one expression or a block. Like let, a closure is a value: you can store it in a binding or hand it to a method.

blocks.title: closures infer their types and see their surroundings

blocks.html:
The parameter and return types of a closure are usually inferred from the first call, which is why |x| x * 2 needs no annotation. A closure also captures: add_offset reads offset from the surrounding scope, and tally writes to calls, which is why tally must be bound with mut. One footnote for later: writing move |x| ... makes the closure take ownership of what it captures instead of borrowing, which matters when the closure has to outlive the current scope.

Now the iterators. There are three ways to walk a collection, and the difference is ownership.

blocks.html: v.iter() lends you &T and leaves v usable afterwards. v.iter_mut() lends you &mut T, so you can write through it. v.into_iter() takes the collection apart and hands you owned T — after that v is gone, which is why nothing touches v again once the last loop has run.

Iterators are lazy. An adapter such as map or filter does no work at all when you call it; it returns a new iterator that carries the recipe. Nothing is visited until a consumer asks for results — collect, sum, count, fold, or a plain for loop.

Watch the order of the lines below: the closure prints only after the adapter is consumed, not when it is built.

blocks.html:
The adapters you will use every week:

  • map — transform each item
  • filter — keep the items whose predicate returns true
  • enumerate — pair each item with its index
  • take(n) — stop after n items
  • zip — glue two iterators into pairs
  • collect — build a Vec, or another collection, from the results

And the consumers that actually run the chain: sum, count, fold. A chain reads left to right the way the data flows. collect needs to know what to build, so give the binding a type: let out: Vec<i32> = ...collect();. The shorthand collect::<Vec<_>>() says the same thing and lets the compiler fill in the element type.

blocks.title: fold, count, and sorting what you collected

blocks.html:
fold is the one that looks odd and is worth knowing: it carries an accumulator through the chain, starting from the value you pass in. sum and count are special cases of it. sort_by_key is a plain method on a Vec, not an adapter, and it sorts in place.

Almost all real iterator code has the shape of the first chain: one source, two or three adapters, one consumer. When a chain grows past that, break it into named steps with let bindings. The compiler is happy either way; the next reader is not.

quiz.q: Which method takes ownership of the vector, so v cannot be used afterwards?
quiz.why: into_iter consumes the collection and yields owned values. iter and iter_mut borrow it and hand out references, so v stays usable.

quiz.q: let loud = v.iter().map(|x| x * 2); — when does that closure run?
options: When a consumer such as collect, sum or a for loop pulls the values
Immediately, as soon as map is called
When the vector is next modified
quiz.why: Adapters are lazy: map only builds a new iterator that remembers the work. The work happens when something consumes it.

options: A closure: a value you can store in a binding or pass to a method
A function declaration that needs a name
quiz.why: The pipes hold the parameters, the expression after them is the body, and the whole thing is an expression you can bind with let, exactly like a number.

exercise.brief: values holds 1 to 5. Use an iterator chain to keep only the even numbers, double each one, and print their total.
exercise.hint: Start with values.into_iter() so the closure receives owned i32 values, then .filter(|n| n % 2 == 0), then .map(|n| n * 2), then .sum(). Give the result a type: let total: i32 = ...
